posts.caption: The new neighbor pulled into our driveway with a plate of banana bread and a lot of questions. She asked if the big mare was friendly, if she bites, and whether she lives outside like a cow. I walked her to the gate and let Big Red take it from there. Big Red inspected the bread, then the neighbor, then the compact car in that order. We've been friends with the neighbor ever since. The banana bread went to the barn cat, who was not consulted either.
posts.first: Years ago a delivery driver backed his truck out of my driveway while Big Red watched from the gate. He stopped, rolled down his window, and said, sorry, ma'am. He wasn't talking to me. I've never needed a guard dog since.

posts.caption: The grass was white and crunchy at six this morning, and the boarder's two-year-old lost his mind at the gate. By the time I got the coffee going he'd done six laps and spooked at his own shadow twice. The old gelding in the next paddock walked out slowly and found the one rectangle of sun against the fence. He closed his eyes. I still had a hose to thaw and a trough to chip. I went and stood next to him for five minutes first.
posts.first: My grandfather used to say the weather turns whether you worry or not. He said it standing at the barn door in a sweater with holes in both elbows. I thought it was a bleak thing to say. I've since stood in a lot of doorways and said it myself.

posts.quote: The round bale lasts nine days. The horses finish it in five and spend the other four acting betrayed.
posts.first: Hay prices went up last month and I stood in the lot looking at the stack like it was a savings account. The horses stood next to me looking at it like a buffet. We were both right about what it was.

posts.caption: Every barn has a rule that nobody follows. Ours is that the small pony does not get treats between meals. My friend Joanne wrote it on a laminated card and taped it to the feed room door in March. She has personally broken it every Saturday since. Last week I found a peppermint in her glove and asked her about it. She said the glove must have picked it up on its own. The pony stood behind her the whole time, perfectly sweet, perfectly silent.
posts.first: Joanne has been boarding with us nine years and has never once admitted to a treat. Last Christmas I found a candy cane taped inside the lid of her tack trunk, labeled for Pudding in her handwriting. I put the lid back down gently and said nothing.

posts.caption: The text said ten minutes. That was at two. By four the sun had moved off the aisle floor and the barn cat had claimed her lap. She came out to drop off a bag of carrots and ended up sitting on a hay bale telling the mare about her week. Her phone buzzed twice in her pocket and she let it. At five her husband texted a photo of the empty driveway with a question mark. She showed me the screen and laughed. Then she sat back down.
posts.first: My husband has a phrase for when I go to the barn and don't come back for a while. He says I've gone to check on the roof. We don't own a barn roof. We've been married twenty-six years and I've never corrected him.

posts.caption: The farm account came due on the first, and I did the math at the kitchen table with a pencil. Feed, farrier, board on the other horse, a vet visit I still don't want to discuss. I put the pencil down at nine and went out to the wash rack to rinse a very expensive mare. She stood perfectly still under the hose and let the water run down her neck. I stood there watching it glitter in the barn light. It was the best nine dollars of water I've ever spent.
posts.first: My husband and I have an agreement about the horse account. He doesn't look at the statement and I don't mention the total. It has worked for twenty-two years. Last month he leaned on the stall door, watched her eat, and said, she looks happy. I put the statement away.
